narrativeReportMd:
# Timing R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No clear hard R4-valid-to-R6-invalid structural break was found for existing `Timing` content: existing local element names, cardinalities, and type domains are preserved. The main risks are R6-to-R4 representability and implementation behavior: R6 adds `repeat.startOffset` and `repeat.endOffset`, expands the required `repeat.when` terminology through a new `IMD` code, and changes computable/semantic guidance around scheduling combinations.

## Scope
The analysis covered the local R4 and R6 `StructureDefinition/Timing` snapshots and differentials, package indexes, package metadata, and directly bound local ValueSets/CodeSystems. Inherited `Element`/`BackboneElement`/`BackboneType` behavior, including the R6 baseDefinition shift to `BackboneType`, is out of scope for local Timing findings.

## Main migration themes
R4-to-R6 migration is mostly additive for the datatype shape. R6-to-R4 conversion is not lossless when R6 instances use `startOffset`, `endOffset`, or `repeat.when = IMD`. Validators and generated models should also be reviewed for the corrected `tim-9` FHIRPath expression and for business rules that were based on R4 comments forbidding `frequency`/`period` with `dayOfWeek` or `timeOfDay`.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest impact findings are `Timing:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:Timing.repeat.startOffset-endOffset:8f9d31` and `Timing:TERMINOLOGY_BINDING:Timing.repeat.when:event-timing-imd:3c4b7e`, both because valid R6 content can carry information that has no direct R4 representation.

## Findings requiring human review
The semantic-text relaxation around `dayOfWeek`/`timeOfDay` combinations deserves human review because it may change locally enforced scheduling rules even though it is not a computable cardinality or type break. The terminology findings would be strengthened by an official expansion and cross-version ConceptMap.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The new offset elements are optional, so the R6 design avoids breaking old R4 instances. The tradeoff is that R6 instances using the new semantics require extension-based or lossy conversion when sent to R4 systems. The `IMD` code addition is similarly non-breaking for R4-to-R6 validation but creates a required-binding round-trip gap for R6-to-R4 exchange.

## Follow-up analysis
Base datatype hierarchy changes should be handled by the `BackboneElement`/`BackboneType` reports. Related Timing extension artifacts should be reviewed separately, especially R4 `timing-dayOfMonth` and `timing-exact`, because they are separate StructureDefinitions rather than local `Timing` elements.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Timing` keeps its existing R4 local element names, cardinalities, and type domains, so no definite hard R4-to-R6 instance break was found. The top migration concerns are R6-only `startOffset`/`endOffset`, R6-only `repeat.when` code `IMD` under a required binding, and semantic/validator changes around repeat scheduling rules. The main uncertainty is terminology expansion and official change-note context.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should treat `Timing` as mostly backward-compatible from R4 to R6 but not losslessly round-trippable from R6 to R4. R6 senders can express interlaced/cyclic schedules with `startOffset` and `endOffset`, and can use `IMD` for immediate timing; R4 receivers need extensions, text, profile-specific conventions, or rejection policies for those cases. Existing validators should be re-tested against `tim-9` and against scheduling combinations involving `dayOfWeek`, `timeOfDay`, `frequency`, and `period`.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural deltas because both assigned StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium-high for terminology because local ValueSet compose and local complete CodeSystems were compared, but no terminology-server expansion, official diff, or ConceptMap was available. Confidence is lower for the practical prevalence of semantic-text changes because that depends on local validation/business-rule behavior.

findings.title: R6 adds Timing.repeat.startOffset and Timing.repeat.endOffset

oldState.summary: R4 Timing.repeat had no startOffset or endOffset elements.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `Timing.repeat` ended at `offset`; interlaced or cyclic schedule offsets had to be represented by other structure, narrative, or extensions.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional `startOffset` and `endOffset`, each `0..1` SimpleQuantity, and constrains each to be used only when `frequency > 1`.

constraints.human: Only use startOffset when frequency is present and > 1
Only use endOffset when frequency is present and > 1

semanticText.short: Events within the repeat period do not start until startOffset has elapsed; events within the repeat period step once endOffset before the end of the period
semanticText.definition: `startOffset` delays events within the repeat period; `endOffset` ends them before the period ends.
semanticText.comment: The R6 comments describe support for interlaced schedules and medication schedules such as doing something for X days and stopping for Y days.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can explicitly express intra-period start and end offsets using SimpleQuantity values. These are new serialized properties under `Timing.repeat` and are guarded by error-level invariants requiring `frequency > 1`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: These are new child elements under the unchanged `Timing.repeat` parent; no R4 element with the same semantics was present in the local Timing snapshot.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break because the elements are optional additions. It is a high R6-to-R4 round-trip risk: R6 instances can now carry scheduling semantics that have no direct R4 core element. Strict R4 parsers, generated R4 classes, JSON schemas, or database schemas may reject or drop the new properties unless an extension or out-of-band mapping is used.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss or misinterpretation of cyclic/interlaced medication timing can change when a therapy is expected to start or stop within a repeat cycle.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent interlaced and cyclic repeat schedules directly in the core Timing datatype.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 less-breaking base-design alternative is needed because the R6 offset elements are optional additions and do not invalidate R4 Timing instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal--representing interlaced or cyclic schedules directly--is supported by the R6 element comments, and the chosen base design adds optional fields under an unchanged parent. That preserves R4-valid instances, so the level of R4-to-R6 breakage is minimal. The remaining risk is that R6 instances using the fields need explicit downgrade handling.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For calibration purposes, ordinary extensions or conversion tooling are mitigations, not a less-breaking R6 base design alternative. A cross-version extension could reduce R6-to-R4 friction, but the base R6 change itself is additive and already preserves existing R4 data.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is an R6-to-R4 downgrade gap; using only extensions would improve cross-version shape compatibility but would sacrifice native R6 discoverability and consistency.

evidence.detail: R4 Timing.repeat has no `startOffset` or `endOffset` child element.
R6 adds `Timing.repeat.startOffset` with cardinality `0..1`, type `Quantity` constrained to SimpleQuantity, and summary flag true.
R6 adds `Timing.repeat.endOffset` with cardinality `0..1`, type `Quantity` constrained to SimpleQuantity, and summary flag true.
R6 adds error-level invariants limiting `startOffset` and `endOffset` to cases where `frequency > 1`.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is a datatype fragment illustrating the new R6 properties. It includes `frequency: 2` so the R6 `tim-11` and `tim-12` invariants are satisfied. R4 has no native `startOffset` or `endOffset` property to receive these values.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds two optional Timing.repeat elements for schedules that start after part of a repeat period has elapsed or stop before the period ends. This does not invalidate existing R4 instances, but it creates a new information channel that R4 systems do not understand. The risk is highest in bidirectional exchange: an R6 schedule can be clinically meaningful yet collapse to a less precise R4 schedule if the offsets are ignored.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid data remains R6-valid with respect to these fields because absent optional elements are still allowed. R6-valid data that uses either field is not cleanly R4-representable as core Timing. R6 validators also enforce that each field appears only when `frequency > 1`, so migrations and test data must not add offsets to one-time-per-period schedules.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6 migration, no transform is required unless existing extensions or local conventions already represented these concepts. For R6-to-R4, define an explicit policy: reject such instances, map them to a documented extension, preserve them in narrative/text, or use a cross-version extension. Test both conformant offset examples and invalid cases where an offset appears without `frequency > 1`.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is structurally additive and therefore the least disruptive core-model approach for R4-to-R6 migration. A cross-version extension would have been more backward compatible for R6-to-R4 exchange, but less likely to be uniformly implemented and harder for generic Timing processors to discover.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds optional `Timing.repeat.startOffset` and `Timing.repeat.endOffset` fields rather than changing or removing any R4 field. That means ordinary R4 Timing instances continue to fit the R6 shape. The real break is reverse-direction and semantic: an R6 dosage or cyclic schedule can now carry offset information that R4 core Timing has no place to store, so a strict R4 parser, generated model, schema, or downgrade mapper may reject or drop clinically relevant timing detail. Given the stated goal of representing interlaced/cyclic schedules directly, the optional core additions look proportionate despite the downgrade burden.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition/Timing has no `Timing.repeat.startOffset` or `Timing.repeat.endOffset` child.
R6 StructureDefinition/Timing adds both fields as `0..1` SimpleQuantity elements with `isSummary=true`.
R6 `Timing.repeat` adds error invariants `tim-11` and `tim-12`, requiring each new offset only when `frequency > 1`.
R6 comments tie these fields to interlaced schedules, Dosage, and medication schedules that cycle on/off.
R4 maturity map and local StructureDefinition show Timing as normative.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Timing is normative, so loss of schedule semantics in medication-oriented use deserves scrutiny. That said, the change does not invalidate R4 instances; the normative status mainly raises the need for explicit downgrade policy rather than making the additive R6 design suspect.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 instances using `startOffset` or `endOffset` have no native R4 core representation, and R4 generated models or validators may reject or discard the new properties.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No clearly better base R6 design was identified. Keeping the concept only in extensions could improve cross-version carrying in R4, but would reduce native R6 discoverability and uniform processing for a core Timing use case; adding optional core fields is already the forward-compatible base-model pattern.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high reverse-direction impact and no hard R4-to-R6 break; agree that extension or mapping strategies are mitigations rather than a clearly less-breaking base R6 design.

findings.title: Required EventTiming binding gains the R6-only IMD code

oldState.summary: R4 `Timing.repeat.when` is a required code binding to `ValueSet/event-timing|4.0.1`; the local FHIR event-timing CodeSystem has 12 codes and no `IMD`.

binding.description: Real world event relating to the schedule.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 ValueSet compose includes all of `http://hl7.org/fhir/event-timing` plus selected v3 TimingEvent codes. The local R4 CodeSystem/event-timing does not define `IMD`.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `when` values must come from the R4 EventTiming value set. In the supplied local CodeSystem, the FHIR event-timing system includes morning/afternoon/evening/night/sleep-related codes, but not `IMD`.

newState.summary: R6 `Timing.repeat.when` remains a required binding but points to `ValueSet/event-timing|6.0.0-ballot4`; the local R6 event-timing CodeSystem adds `IMD` for immediate timing.

binding.description: Real-world event relating to the schedule.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 ValueSet compose still includes all of `http://hl7.org/fhir/event-timing`; the local R6 CodeSystem adds `IMD`, so the required binding permits an R6 value not present in the R4 local CodeSystem.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `IMD` with display `Immediate` and definition indicating a single occurrence as soon as possible after the scheduled or actual start of the overall event.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same local element `Timing.repeat.when` exists in both releases with the same primitive type and required binding strength; the material delta is the versioned value set/code-system content.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using old EventTiming codes remain within the R6 binding. The break is in the reverse direction: a valid R6 instance can use required-binding code `IMD`, but an R4 validator using the R4 value set will reject it or treat it as outside the required domain. Generated enum switches and decision logic that assume the R4 EventTiming code list can also fail or fall through.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Immediate/as-soon-as-possible scheduling semantics can affect urgency and timing of medication or care actions if dropped or mapped imprecisely.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent an immediate one-time timing event directly in the EventTiming code system.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 less-breaking base-design alternative is needed because R6 widens the required EventTiming vocabulary without removing R4-valid codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding `IMD` is a normal way to represent a newly standardized timing concept, and the local evidence shows the old R4 EventTiming codes remain available while R6 adds the immediate timing code. This does not make R4 instances invalid in R6. The compatibility concern is R6-to-R4 validation, enum handling, and downgrade policy.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: This is a forward terminology widening, so the backward-compatible-alternative question is not applicable for R4-to-R6 base design. Avoiding the code or keeping it only as text/local extension would reduce downgrade friction but would fail the R6 goal of making immediate timing a first-class required-binding code. An official ConceptMap would be useful migration guidance, not a less-breaking R6 base shape.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The material cost is reverse-direction terminology handling for R4 receivers; ConceptMaps or extensions help downgrade but are mitigations rather than base-design alternatives.

evidence.detail: The local R6 CodeSystem/event-timing includes code `IMD` with display `Immediate`.
evidence.quote: Event occurs a single time (with no repetitions) as soon as possible after the scheduled or actual start of the overall event.

evidence.detail: The local R4 CodeSystem/event-timing contains 12 codes and does not contain `IMD`.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is valid only if the R6 required EventTiming binding includes `IMD`. An R4 terminology validator using the local R4 value set/code system would not find this code in the required binding.

findings.narrativeMd: `Timing.repeat.when` keeps the same element shape, but its required terminology domain expands in R6. The added `IMD` code is useful for immediate timing, but it means that a syntactically small R6 Timing can carry a required-binding code that R4 does not know. This is primarily a round-trip and receiver compatibility issue rather than an R4-to-R6 break.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old R4 values are not made invalid by this change. An R6 instance using `when: ["IMD"]` is R6-valid under the R6 binding but not R4-valid under the local R4 required binding. Runtime effects include enum exhaustiveness failures, terminology validation failures, and lossy downgrade transforms.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, no action is needed for existing codes. For R6-to-R4, add explicit handling for `IMD`: reject it, preserve it in an extension, map it to narrative/text, or apply a locally governed code mapping if one exists. Test downgrade paths with `IMD` and with mixed `when` arrays containing both old and new codes.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The code addition is a standard forward evolution of a required code system. A backward-compatible alternative would require a cross-version extension or official ConceptMap rather than avoiding the new code entirely. Without such guidance, R4 compatibility remains a local policy decision.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `Timing.repeat.when` keeps the same path, cardinality, primitive type, and required binding strength, but the R6 EventTiming code system includes a new `IMD` code for immediate timing. Existing R4 codes are not removed, so this is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break. The compatibility issue is that an R6 instance using `IMD` can fail R4 required-binding validation or generated-enum handling. Adding a first-class code for a real scheduling concept is a reasonable terminology evolution, provided cross-version receivers make an explicit policy for `IMD`.
keyEvidence: R4 `Timing.repeat.when` is bound required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/event-timing|4.0.1`.
R6 `Timing.repeat.when` is bound required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/event-timing|6.0.0-ballot4`.
R4 CodeSystem/event-timing contains 12 codes and no `IMD`.
R6 CodeSystem/event-timing adds `IMD` with display `Immediate` and definition for a single event as soon as possible after the scheduled or actual start.
Both R4 and R6 EventTiming ValueSets include all codes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/event-timing`, so the new code enters the required binding through the code system expansion.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The Timing datatype and EventTiming terminology are normative in the local R4 inputs, which raises the burden to avoid gratuitous code-domain churn. Here the old required-domain values remain available, so the maturity concern is mostly about documenting reverse mapping, not about rejecting the R6 addition.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R4 terminology validators, switch statements, and generated enums may not accept `IMD`; downgrade requires rejection, text preservation, extension use, or a governed local mapping.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No equivalent less-breaking base R6 design is apparent. Avoiding `IMD` or leaving immediate timing only as text/local coding would reduce downgrade friction but would not standardize the concept in the required EventTiming domain. ConceptMaps are useful migration guidance but not a base-model alternative.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high R6-to-R4 risk and agree that no less-breaking base design is obvious; the high impact should be read as reverse-direction terminology compatibility, not as R4 data becoming invalid in R6.

findings.title: tim-9 offset/when invariant expression was rewritten for multi-valued when

constraints.human: If there's an offset, there must be a when (and not C, CM, CD, CV)

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 already had an error-level rule saying that `offset` requires `when` and cannot be used with `C`, `CM`, `CD`, or `CV`. The computable expression used a direct `when in (...)` test over a repeatable element.

newState.summary: R6 keeps the same human rule but uses `when.select($this in ('C' | 'CM' | 'CD' | 'CV')).allFalse()`.

constraints.human: If there's an offset, there must be a when (and not C, CM, CD, CV)

newState.narrativeMd: R6 expresses the same prohibition using a per-item selection and `allFalse()`, which is clearer for `when` arrays with more than one value.

facts.oldValue: If there's an offset, there must be a when (and not C, CM, CD, CV)
facts.newValue: If there's an offset, there must be a when (and not C, CM, CD, CV)

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The invariant key and human text match across releases; only the computable FHIRPath expression changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The normative human rule did not change, so this is not a clear old-valid/new-invalid semantic change. However, the R6 FHIRPath is more explicit for multi-valued `when`; an R4 validator that mishandled the repeatable `when in (...)` expression may have accepted instances that an R6 validator rejects. The practical impact is therefore validator/runtime compatibility rather than a definite model break.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The affected pattern is narrow: `offset` plus one of the meal timing codes that the invariant excludes.

justification.inferredGoal: Correct or clarify the computable expression for a repeatable `when` element while preserving the same human invariant.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking computable expression was identified that still enforces the unchanged `tim-9` rule consistently for repeated `when` values.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The human invariant did not change: `offset` still requires `when` and excludes `C`, `CM`, `CD`, and `CV`. R6 rewrites the FHIRPath to apply that unchanged rule clearly across repeated `when` values. Any compatibility impact is therefore limited to data or tooling that depended on the older expression's collection ambiguity, making the rewrite probably reasonable despite the potential validation surprise.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Retaining the R4 FHIRPath would be less disruptive only for validators that interpreted the ambiguous collection expression permissively. It would not meet the same goal of consistent computable enforcement. A warning-level transition could reduce surprise, but it would weaken an error-level invariant whose human wording was already present in R4.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping the R4 expression would preserve some validator behavior but perpetuate ambiguous or inconsistent enforcement of the same human rule.

evidence.detail: R4 uses a direct `when in (...)` expression.
R6 uses `when.select(...).allFalse()` for the prohibited code check.

examples.examplesMd: A fragment such as `{"repeat":{"when":["AC","C"],"offset":30}}` is not presented as R4-valid because the R4 human rule already forbids `C` with `offset`. It is an example of the kind of multi-valued `when` array where validator behavior could differ after the computable expression rewrite.

findings.narrativeMd: The `tim-9` invariant still says the same thing in English: if `offset` exists, `when` must exist and must not be one of `C`, `CM`, `CD`, or `CV`. R6 rewrites the FHIRPath to evaluate each `when` repetition explicitly. Implementers may see new validation failures if their R4 tooling treated the old collection expression as permissive or indeterminate.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no definite R4-valid/new-invalid example from the StructureDefinitions alone because the R4 human rule already prohibited the target pattern. The compatibility risk is that computable validation behavior can become stricter or more consistent in R6 for multi-valued `when` arrays. R6-to-R4 representation is not materially affected.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review test data and production data for `Timing.repeat.offset` combined with `when` values `C`, `CM`, `CD`, or `CV`, especially arrays containing both allowed and disallowed values. Update custom FHIRPath validators and unit tests to use the R6 expression semantics rather than relying on the old expression form.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Since the human rule did not change, preserving the old expression would mainly preserve ambiguity. The compatible migration path is to clean data and align validators, not to map fields.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The `tim-9` human rule remains the same in R6: if `offset` is present, `when` must be present and must not be `C`, `CM`, `CD`, or `CV`. The changed FHIRPath expression appears to make the repeated-code test explicit rather than changing the intended conformance rule. A system that previously accepted `offset` with a prohibited meal-timing code may see a new validation failure, but that would be enforcement of a rule already stated in R4, not a legitimate R4-valid/new-R6-invalid data pattern.
keyEvidence: R4 `Timing.repeat` constraint `tim-9` has severity `error` and human text forbidding offset with `C`, `CM`, `CD`, or `CV`.
R4 `tim-9` expression used `((when in ('C' | 'CM' | 'CD' | 'CV')).not())` against repeatable `when`.
R6 `tim-9` keeps the same severity and human text.
R6 rewrites the expression to `when.select($this in ('C' | 'CM' | 'CD' | 'CV')).allFalse()`.
`Timing.repeat.when` is repeatable (`0..*`) in both R4 and R6.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative status raises scrutiny for constraint changes, but it also makes preservation of the stated R4 rule important. Because the human error-level invariant did not change, FMM/status does not support treating this as a standards-design break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: validator behavior may become more consistent for multi-valued `when`, but the affected instances were already contrary to the R4 human invariant; no clear old-valid/new-invalid base instance break exists.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Retaining the older collection expression would be less disruptive only for permissive or inconsistent validators, and would preserve ambiguity. Downgrading to a warning would weaken an error-level rule already present in R4. No better less-breaking base expression was identified.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing potential hard-break characterization and medium impact; agree only that validator behavior can change and that preserving the old expression is not a good alternative.

findings.title: R6 removes R4 comment text that discouraged frequency/period with dayOfWeek or timeOfDay

oldState.summary: R4 comments said `frequency` and `period` cannot be used with `dayOfWeek`, and `when`, `frequency`, and `period` cannot be used with `timeOfDay`.

semanticText.comment: dayOfWeek: If no days are specified, the action is assumed to happen every day as otherwise specified. The elements frequency and period cannot be used as well as dayOfWeek. timeOfDay: When time of day is specified, it is inferred that the action happens every day (as filtered by dayofWeek) on the specified times. The elements when, frequency and period cannot be used as well as timeOfDay.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 carried non-invariant comment text that many implementers could reasonably read as a conformance rule against combining day/time filters with `frequency` and `period`.

newState.summary: R6 removes the `frequency`/`period` prohibition from `dayOfWeek` and narrows the `timeOfDay` comment to the existing `timeOfDay` versus `when` rule.

semanticText.comment: dayOfWeek: If no days are specified, the action is assumed to happen every day as otherwise specified. timeOfDay: When time of day is specified, it is inferred that the action happens every day (as filtered by dayofWeek) on the specified times. If there's a timeOfDay, there cannot be a when, or vice versa.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 no longer says that `frequency` and `period` are incompatible with `dayOfWeek` or `timeOfDay`; the remaining computable prohibition is `timeOfDay.empty() or when.empty()`.

facts.oldValue: If no days are specified, the action is assumed to happen every day as otherwise specified. The elements frequency and period cannot be used as well as dayOfWeek.
facts.newValue: If no days are specified, the action is assumed to happen every day as otherwise specified.

facts.oldValue: When time of day is specified, it is inferred that the action happens every day (as filtered by dayofWeek) on the specified times. The elements when, frequency and period cannot be used as well as timeOfDay.
facts.newValue: When time of day is specified, it is inferred that the action happens every day (as filtered by dayofWeek) on the specified times. If there's a timeOfDay, there cannot be a when, or vice versa.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a hard validation break because the R4 text was a comment rather than a distinct invariant, and R6 relaxes rather than tightens the stated rule. The runtime risk is that systems that encoded the R4 comment as a business rule may reject or transform R6 schedules that combine `frequency`/`period` with `dayOfWeek` or `timeOfDay`. Conversely, R4-to-R6 migration may reveal local rule differences rather than schema differences.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Frequency/period/day/time combinations are common in medication and care schedules; inconsistent interpretation can alter the intended schedule.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that `dayOfWeek` and `timeOfDay` can filter or qualify repeat schedules while retaining the explicit `timeOfDay` versus `when` exclusion.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 less-breaking base-design alternative is needed because R6 relaxes non-invariant comment guidance rather than invalidating R4 Timing instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The StructureDefinitions show a semantic-text relaxation: R6 removes comment text discouraging `frequency`/`period` combinations while retaining the computable `timeOfDay` versus `when` exclusion. Because the old restriction was not a distinct invariant and R6 does not make old instances invalid, the level of base-design breakage is low. Local validators and schedulers may still need review, but the inferred clarification goal is reasonable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The alternative of keeping the R4 warning text is transitional guidance, not a necessary less-breaking base R6 design for preserving R4 instances. It might have helped implementers notice the change, but it would also risk preserving an over-restrictive interpretation that the R6 text appears to be correcting.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Retaining legacy warning text could reduce surprise for local R4-derived business rules, but it would continue ambiguity about combinations R6 intends to allow.

evidence.detail: R4 says frequency and period cannot be used with dayOfWeek.
R6 removes the frequency/period incompatibility sentence from the dayOfWeek comment.
R4 says when, frequency, and period cannot be used with timeOfDay.
R6 narrows the comment to the `timeOfDay` versus `when` exclusion.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment uses only R4-known fields, so the issue is semantic rather than syntactic. A strict R4-derived business rule based on the old comments could reject it, while R6 no longer carries the same frequency/period prohibition.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 changes the descriptive guidance for common repeat scheduling fields. The old R4 comments discouraged combining `frequency`/`period` with `dayOfWeek` and `timeOfDay`; R6 removes that prohibition and leaves the explicit `timeOfDay` versus `when` rule. This can surprise systems that converted the R4 comments into validation or scheduling logic.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: FHIR instance validation based strictly on min/max/type/binding is not broken. Compatibility risk appears in semantic validators, generated rule engines, and scheduling algorithms. R6 content using combinations that R4 comments discouraged can be serialized in R4 shape but may not be semantically acceptable to R4-era implementations.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory custom Timing validators and scheduling logic for rules that reject `dayOfWeek` with `frequency`/`period` or `timeOfDay` with `frequency`/`period`. Decide whether to keep those restrictions as local profile rules or relax them for R6. Add test cases for weekly day/time schedules and for invalid `timeOfDay` plus `when` combinations.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the old restriction was comment text rather than an invariant, R6 could change the guidance without a formal schema break. A backward-compatible alternative would have been to retain legacy warning text for one release, but that might have continued an overly restrictive interpretation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 removes R4 comment text that said `frequency` and `period` cannot be combined with `dayOfWeek`, and narrows the `timeOfDay` comment to the existing computable `timeOfDay` versus `when` exclusion. Cardinalities, types, and the `tim-10` invariant do not tighten. This may require local validators or scheduling engines that encoded the old comments as hard rules to be updated, but it is a relaxation/clarification rather than an R4-to-R6 instance break.
keyEvidence: R4 `Timing.repeat.dayOfWeek.comment` says `frequency` and `period` cannot be used as well as `dayOfWeek`.
R6 `Timing.repeat.dayOfWeek.comment` removes that incompatibility sentence.
R4 `Timing.repeat.timeOfDay.comment` says `when`, `frequency`, and `period` cannot be used as well as `timeOfDay`.
R6 `Timing.repeat.timeOfDay.comment` only states that `timeOfDay` and `when` cannot both be present.
`tim-10` remains `timeOfDay.empty() or when.empty()` in R6, and the affected element cardinalities/types remain stable.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Timing is normative, so semantic text changes should be checked rather than dismissed. The actual mechanism is a non-computable relaxation with stable field shape, so normative status does not make this a material breaking design issue.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: R4-derived business rules may differ from R6 guidance, but base structural validation is not tightened and old R4 instances are not made invalid.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Keeping the R4 prohibition as transitional prose might reduce surprise for local validators, but it would also preserve guidance R6 appears to be correcting. Adding a formal invariant would be more breaking, not less. No necessary less-breaking base R6 design is apparent.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that local scheduling logic deserves migration awareness; disagree with treating this as medium-impact break or requiring design reconsideration, because it is a relaxation of comment text rather than a hard compatibility break.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, abstract flag, and active status are stable. The baseDefinition shift is intentionally excluded as an inherited/base infrastructure topic.
No existing local Timing element changed minimum or maximum cardinality. R6 adds optional elements only.

Existing local element types and the `bounds[x]` choice domain (`Duration`, `Range`, `Period`) are unchanged. The only new type surface is the added `startOffset`/`endOffset` SimpleQuantity elements, which are covered as a finding.
`Timing` has no local `Reference`-typed elements in either release.
No local Timing element changed `isModifier`; the added R6 offset elements are not modifiers. Inherited `modifierExtension` behavior is out of scope.
Existing local summary flags are unchanged. The added `startOffset` and `endOffset` are summary elements, which is noted in the element-addition finding.
No local Timing slicing definitions were introduced, removed, or changed. Inherited extension slicing is excluded as base behavior.
No local Timing element gained or lost a fixed value, pattern value, or default value.
No local `minValue`, `maxValue`, `maxLength`, or regex limit changes were found. Numeric primitive domains such as `positiveInt`, `unsignedInt`, and `decimal` remain the same on existing elements.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Preferred TimingAbbreviation value set now includes C for continuous frequency
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Timing.code` is a `CodeableConcept` with a `preferred` binding, not a required primitive-code binding. R4 instances are not made invalid, and R4 can still carry a CodeableConcept using an unfamiliar coding system, though terminology validation may not consider it preferred.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: R6 adds `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/timing-abbreviation` with code `C` (`Continuous (frequency)`) and updates the `Timing.code` short text from `BID | TID | ...` to `C | BID | TID | ...`. Code generators or UI picklists derived from the preferred value set should add `C`; R6-to-R4 downgrade may need text or local mapping if R4 systems expect only v3-GTSAbbreviation codes.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 clarifies that UCUM mo is normally used as a calendar month for next-occurrence calculation
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element types, cardinalities, required binding strength, and allowed UCUM unit codes did not change; the local `units-of-time` ValueSet compose is the same in R4 and R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Scheduling engines should review how they interpret `mo`. The R6 definition adds normal-practice guidance that `mo` is used as a calendar month when calculating the next occurrence, which can matter for end-of-month and variable-month-length schedules.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: UnitsOfTime and DaysOfWeek binding URLs advance to R6 versions with no local code-set change found
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The bindings remain `required`, but the local ValueSet compose/code-system comparison found the same UCUM time unit codes (`s`, `min`, `h`, `d`, `wk`, `mo`, `a`) and the same seven days-of-week codes in R4 and R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology caches should refresh versioned canonical references from `|4.0.1` to `|6.0.0-ballot4`, but no value mapping is indicated by the local package artifacts.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 `Timing` specializes `BackboneType` instead of R4 `BackboneElement`. Per the inherited/base-artifact scope rule, class-hierarchy and inherited extension/modifier behavior should be owned by the base datatype reports.

The R4 package contains Timing-related extension StructureDefinitions that were not present in the R6 package index checked here. They are separate artifacts rather than local `Timing` elements, but systems using those extensions on `Timing.repeat` need a separate migration assessment.
The R6-only `IMD` code in a required binding needs official or local mapping guidance for downgrade workflows.
